POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Tue, 03 Nov 2026 23:43:07 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 EU tells Ukraine to hasten reforms, sets out more cautious path for accession https://www.politico.eu/article/ukraine-accession-path-eu-membership-wobbles-european-commission-brussels-caution/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 03 Nov 2026 23:26:22 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9265791 BRUSSELS — The European Commission is preparing a more cautious roadmap for Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations, setting out limited targets for progress in 2027 while avoiding any commitment to a membership date, according to a document obtained by POLITICO.

Brussels has long sought to bring Ukraine closer to the EU in a broader effort to secure its future after Russia’s war, with eventual membership seen as a way to anchor Kyiv firmly in European institutions and make renewed Russian aggression more difficult.

In the document, Brussels calls on Kyiv to “urgently and significantly step up the pace of the rule of law reforms.” Meeting key requirements in this area in the first half of 2027 is necessary before negotiations in individual policy areas can be provisionally concluded, the roadmap says.

The document, part of the Commission’s enlargement package to be presented Wednesday, identifies seven policy areas in which Ukraine could provisionally complete negotiations next year. It highlights how far Ukraine still has to go before joining the bloc — and the difficulty of delivering the necessary reforms while fighting a war.

Decoupling from Moldova

The document also underscores a growing divergence between Ukraine and Moldova, whose membership bids have long advanced in parallel. Moldova is now seen as being in a position to make substantially faster progress, raising the prospect that the two countries’ membership bids will effectively be decoupled.

While Brussels is targeting progress in seven policy areas for Ukraine in 2027, Moldova could complete negotiations in more than 20, the document shows.

Ukraine applied to join the EU on Feb. 28, 2022, just four days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. Moldova and Ukraine secured candidate status together in June 2022 and formally launched membership negotiations on the same day in June 2024.

Since then, Kyiv has completed a detailed examination of how its laws compare with EU rules and negotiations have formally opened across several major policy areas. In October, Ukraine and Moldova both opened talks covering the EU’s internal market, competitiveness and economic growth.

A long way to go

Joining the EU requires far more than a political commitment. Candidate countries must bring their laws and institutions into line with EU standards across 35 negotiating areas, known in Brussels jargon as chapters. These range from agriculture and food safety to competition rules, judicial independence and foreign policy.

The Commission’s roadmap identifies only seven such areas in which Ukraine could provisionally finish negotiations in 2027. Education and culture is targeted for the first half of the year, followed by intellectual property, employment and social policy, industrial policy, research, external relations, and foreign and security policy in the second half.

The Commission acknowledges that the changes are complex and require extensive consultations, time and resources. To help Ukraine make progress, Brussels has established a dedicated task force to provide additional support to Ukrainian authorities.

The difficulties are compounded by the war, which places extraordinary demands on Ukraine’s government and parliament as they seek to pass and implement the legislation required for EU membership.

The Commission is careful in the document not to commit to an end date for Ukraine’s accession negotiations, taking a similarly cautious approach toward other EU membership frontrunners, including Albania and Moldova. Montenegro is the exception, with June 2027 envisaged as a target for signing an accession treaty.

Ukraine’s roadmap describes itself as a “living document” that can be updated as talks progress, leaving open the possibility of completing negotiations in additional policy areas sooner if reforms advance faster than expected.

The shadow of war

The uncertainty also reflects the wider challenge of admitting a country still fighting an existential war.

EU rules do not explicitly prohibit a country at war from becoming a member, but Ukraine’s accession would raise difficult questions about security, territory and the obligations EU countries would assume toward a fellow member under the bloc’s mutual assistance provisions.

Even a peace settlement would not automatically resolve those questions or remove the need for Ukraine to complete its reforms. And finishing negotiations in individual policy areas would still leave Kyiv facing further steps before membership, including an accession treaty requiring approval and ratification.

The Commission also wants talks on Ukraine’s two stalled negotiating clusters to begin by the end of 2026. These are cluster 4, covering the green agenda and sustainable connectivity, and cluster 5, covering resources, agriculture and cohesion.

The document states that the Commission considers Ukraine to have met the necessary conditions and urges the accession conference to make every effort to open the outstanding clusters before the end of the year.

Opening them would allow Ukraine to advance negotiations across the remaining policy areas, although the pace of subsequent progress will remain dependent on reforms and the relevant decisions by member countries.

]]> en Spain’s transport minister resigns after deadly train crash https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-transport-minister-oscar-puente-resigns-after-deadly-train-crash/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 03 Nov 2026 21:23:48 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9266379 MADRID — Óscar Puente, Spain’s transport minister and a close ally of Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, resigned on Tuesday night just over a week after a rail disaster that has shocked the country.

His resignation came after an hours-long grilling by the Spanish parliament’s standing committee, which is acting on behalf of the parliament while it is dissolved ahead of the Nov. 29 snap election.

“My decision is a matter of political dignity,” Puente said, adding that it was the right call for “a modern country, not a failed state as some claim.”

Puente has been cornered by allies and foes alike, who called for him to step down after last week’s train crash, in which 69 people died. It was the second deadly rail disaster in Spain this year after January’s accident in Adamuz, which killed 46 people. Puente had held the post since 2023.

“Puente stood up, stepped up and then stepped aside,” wrote Sánchez in a message on social media. “While some only give lectures, others give it their all,” added the prime minister. Puente had been one of Sánchez’s most trusted lieutenants in taking on the opposition.

Sánchez had backed Puente after the Toledo crash raised questions about how Spain manages its rail infrastructure and dealt a blow to his reelection hopes.

Puente said he made the decision to resign in the moments after the accident — in sharp contrast with statements last week in which he strongly denied he would stand down.

On Oct. 30 he said resigning would be “the easy option.” After a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday morning, Puente brushed off calls for his resignation from some of the government’s allies, including members of Sumar, the coalition’s junior partner.

Government sources had ruled out that scenario as recently as Tuesday afternoon: “He’s not going to resign, and we’re not going to dismiss him.”

Ester Muñoz, the People’s Party parliamentary chief, said that “The resignation comes 116 lives too late,” referencing the lives lost in the two high-profile rail disasters as well as a train driver who died in a separate accident in Catalonia this year.

In increasingly heated exchanges, Nawrocki accused Tusk of using the court dispute for an illegal power grab, while Tusk defended his actions as vital to preserving the rule of law in the EU’s sixth-largest economy.

The long-running but highly charged judicial dispute dates back more than a decade and centers on the political appointment of judges at the top court by the previous administration of the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party that was in power until 2023.

Tusk’s government and the European Commission have insisted the court must be overhauled to conform with EU norms on impartiality, and on Friday suspended the court’s president and his deputy.

On Tuesday, eight judges elected by the current ruling majority led by Tusk convened the court and declared they had sufficient numbers to resume its long-stalled work.

Hitting back, Nawrocki used the televised opening of a National Security Council meeting, attended by Tusk and other political leaders, to attack the prime minister. Tusk was not given a chance to respond while the cameras were on.

“Full responsibility for every police officer outside the tribunal, for all the illegal actions, including suspending judges and issuing unlawful orders, lies with one man who is present in this room — Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” Nawrocki said, referring to Friday’s confrontations in front of the tribunal.

“I expect [the prime minister] to rein in his government’s ambitions and put an end to the illegal actions of his representatives inside the Constitutional Tribunal,” Nawrocki added.

Earlier, Tusk had accused Nawrocki of escalating the conflict and called on him to end his opposition to the judges elected by parliament.

“The president has a chance, and I hope he takes it, to stop attacking lawfully elected tribunal judges and allow them to work,” Tusk said before a Cabinet meeting.

Tusk also accused Moscow of exploiting Poland’s political turmoil and urged politicians not to become “useful idiots” as the squabble over the court’s fate intensifies.

As the National Security Council meeting ended, Tusk reiterated his main points on the tribunal but adopted a more conciliatory tone, offering Nawrocki a one-on-one meeting to “think about how to reduce tension.”

But he also said he was pleased that the “situation was stabilizing,” alluding to the fait accompli of the tribunal having resumed work. 

The feud over the tribunal is hardening Poland’s political divisions ahead of the 2027 parliamentary election, bringing a previously divided array of factions on the nationalist right into closer alignment against Tusk. For the prime minister, the crisis also serves as an opportunity to consolidate the voter base ahead of the election.

The eight judges elected by the current parliamentary majority held a general assembly Tuesday afternoon under Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge who assumed control of the court Friday. Nawrocki and the right-wing camp do not recognize her authority.

The president also keeps refusing to swear in five of the eight judges. Instead, they took their oaths in the parliament in a ceremony that Nawrocki contends was null and void.

The eight voted to recognize themselves as a quorum, arguing that only 12 of the court’s 15 judges were eligible to participate after Korwin-Piotrowska temporarily suspended PiS-linked Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański. A third PiS-era appointee, Jarosław Wyrembak, occupied an improperly filled seat.

That reduced the required two-thirds quorum from 10 to eight, although Święczkowski and his political allies rejected his suspension and the quorum calculation.

The judges unanimously approved the tribunal’s draft budget for 2027 and drew names for disciplinary panels to consider proceedings against Święczkowski and Sochański.

Until September, Trump had repeatedly pushed for the U.S. to take control of the large, mineral-rich island, which is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, citing national security reasons.

His fixation on the idea, and his repeated refusals to rule out using military force to take the territory — as well as his use of tariffs against allied countries he saw as standing in his way — stretched the NATO alliance close to breaking point.

“Europe must and wants to play a role in this process,” said Merz alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin Tuesday. “Key elements of a peaceful solution — whether regarding sanctions or the security architecture — can only be resolved with us Europeans. And everyone involved knows that very well.”

Zelenskyy also suggested that no peace deal could be struck that would preclude his country from joining the EU and benefiting from what he called the bloc’s “security infrastructure.”

“The U.S. and Russia — with all due respect to the U.S. — cannot decide whether Ukraine will become a member state of the European Union,” Zelenskyy said. “For that we need the support of other countries, and all of those countries are in Europe.”

Merz’s meeting with Zelenskyy in Berlin comes as the Trump administration renews efforts to reach a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine and before U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia are set to resume in Abu Dhabi next week.

The meeting in Berlin also comes a day before talks hosted by the European Commission with representatives from the U.S., Ukraine and key European allies on Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic future.

Merz also sharply criticized the U.S. decision to invite Russian President Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 summit in Miami, saying the move is shutting Ukraine out of talks about its own fate.

“If President Trump were to decide to invite the Russian president, then Ukraine must be the first topic of discussion,” Merz said. “And if Ukraine is discussed, then the president of Ukraine must be seated at the table. In any case, from my perspective, it is completely unacceptable for third countries to discuss Ukraine’s fate without involving Ukraine itself.”

European leaders, including Merz, have long feared the U.S. may pursue a Ukraine peace deal on terms that sideline Europe and disadvantage Ukraine.

Merz said his government is moving to provide Ukraine with additional aid to help get it through the winter and urged allies to up their support, adding: “All Europeans share the responsibility — not just the Germans.”

The chancellor also said Germany had invited European and international leaders allied with Ukraine to Berlin for a Nov. 19 “Coalition of the Willing” meeting to agree on additional military support for Kyiv and “affirm our willingness to provide security guarantees” in the event of a ceasefire.

Zelenskyy also said the two leaders discussed further assistance to address severe shortages in Ukrainian air defense systems, specifically a lack of interceptor missiles. He also said the leaders discussed a new support package for Ukraine’s fleet of U.S.-made F-16 fighter jets.

Speaking later at the Berlin Security Conference, Zelenskyy urged European leaders to strengthen the continent’s defenses, warning that U.S. politics were turning increasingly inward.

“The U.S. role in the world may become even smaller, so Europe’s role in the world must become even greater,” he said. “And without Germany, this is impossible.”

Zelenskyy added a stark warning.

“Look at the military infrastructure Russia has been building in recent years,” he said. “Is all that just for Ukraine? It’s too much to be just for one country, for Ukraine. It’s aimed at you.”

Chris Lunday contributed reporting.

This story has been updated.

]]> en The 5 most brutal political moggings of 2026 https://www.politico.eu/article/the-5-most-brutal-political-moggings-of-2026/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 03 Nov 2026 14:34:49 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9262803

The 5 most brutal political moggings of 2026

From Vladimir Putin to Donald Trump, some of the world’s most powerful leaders have been outshone this year.

By POLITICO

Photo-illustration by Natália Delgado/POLITICO (source images via Getty)

Boomers, look away now. 

The Collins English Dictionary announced its 2026 word of the year Tuesday morning, with judges opting for “mogging.” 

For readers not fluent in youth culture: Mogging “might involve making [anyone] look inferior in terms of appearance, confidence or status — anything, really,” according to marketing consultant and copywriter Rachel Quin, who authored a Collins article announcing the winner.

According to Collins, the term originated in the bodybuilding community as a shortening of AMOG (“alpha male of the group”) and penetrated into the so-called manosphere, a collection of typically online male communities united by their beliefs about masculinity.

“Fast forward to 2026 and it’s everywhere,” Quin added. And, crucially for POLITICO’s purposes, it can be applied to literally any situation. 

With that in mind, we looked back at five top political moggings in 2026 — the more brutal, the better. 

Andy Burnham job mogged Keir Starmer 

One minute, Keir Starmer was British prime minister with a thumping Labour majority cheering his every move. The next, he was humiliated and ousted by a northern rival who had done little to hide his own leadership ambitions. 

Starmer, of course, tried to block the Downing Street takeover by Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham.

But once Burnham loyalists and grumpy ministers had quit Starmer’s government in droves, the prime minister bowed out this summer after just two years in office and Burnham — having manufactured, at the second attempt, an opportunity to enter parliament — waltzed into the top job unopposed. 

Daniel Chapo frame mogged Vladimir Putin 

Call it the textbook framemog. 

Mozambique’s towering president, Daniel Chapo — who stands more than two meters tall — loomed over tiny Russian leader Vladimir Putin at a summit between African countries and Russia in Moscow last week.

Countries signed a summit declaration pledging to expand “cooperation in energy, minerals, and digital technology, establishing Russian industrial zones in Africa, and localizing production” — but the defining image of the summit was a photo of Chapo dwarfing Putin.

Looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular, real name Braden Peters, likely breathed a sigh of relief, having suffered the year’s other most notorious framemogging, at the hands of internet character “ASU frat leader.”

Jacob Rees-Mogg debate mogged Tucker Carlson

In a classic case of nominative determinism, Jacob Rees-Mogg, former British government minister and current haunted pencil, pantsed American commentator Tucker Carlson in a discussion on the latter’s YouTube channel in October.

Rees-Mogg may not have expected to find himself defending Britain’s decision to fight against Adolf Hitler, but that’s what happened after Carlson questioned why Britain had even bothered entering World War II against Nazi Germany.

Rees-Mogg said he was very surprised that Carlson was “verging on defending Hitler,” adding: “I think this is not really what you want to be doing,” in a clip that went viral and catapulted the Brexit hard-liner back into the British public consciousness. 

The algae scum mogged Donald Trump 

Donald Trump’s bid to clean out the iconic Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C. was initially hampered by persistent pond scum. 

After a money-spinning renovation in early summer, algae came back with a vengeance, turning the water green and murky, while the blue paint job began to peel off the pool bottom. 

Rather than turn his ire toward the contractors, Trump blamed vandals for attacking the pool, and his Department of Justice attempted to prosecute people it accused of damaging the site. Judges, however, dropped or dismissed the criminal cases.

Trump returned to the theme Monday — right before America went to the polls for midterm elections in which the country is laser-focused on the surging cost of living and corruption — holding a rally in front of the pool and recounting all the issues he said he’d fixed with the pool, including “tremendous algae.”

Péter Magyar poll mogged Viktor Orbán

In Hungary’s biggest aura battle ever, conservative challenger Péter Magyar defeated longtime nationalist leader Viktor Orbán, ending 16 years in power for the populist prime minister. 

Magyar, a former MP for Orbán’s Fidesz party, dramatically broke ranks in 2024, releasing a tape of his ex-wife apparently incriminating members of Orbán’s inner circle in a corruption scandal when she was justice minister. For two years, he consistently attacked Fidesz and Orbán over graft while building a movement to take down the EU’s problem child. 

Magyar ultimately led a big-tent campaign focusing on cost-of-living concerns and pro-EU messaging, which turned into a landslide election victory that left Trump and the Kremlin salty.

The meeting would take place at the upcoming APEC summit on Nov. 18–19 in Shenzhen, China, which the three leaders are scheduled to attend. Putin publicly welcomed the prospect on Sunday, noting that it would depend “to a large extent” on the Chinese hosts.

“There is a common understanding among the participants in such a potential meeting that it would be appropriate and highly useful. Work is underway to coordinate such a meeting,” Peskov told reporters on Tuesday. “We hope that it will be finalized in the coming days,” he added.

Trump told reporters last month he would meet Putin and Xi, initially “on denuclearization,” but also to discuss Ukraine. “I would meet in order — anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody is there or not, whatever I can do to end the war.”

Kyiv met the prospect of a trilateral meeting with concern, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy stressing that it should take place after a meeting that includes Ukraine. “I really don’t want this to be a ‘Yalta – 2, 3, 4,’ when there is a redistribution of influence,” Zelenskyy told reporters in late October — referring to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the U.S., British and Soviet leaders agreed on aspects of the postwar settlement in Europe, including the occupation of Germany.

China has not commented on the possibility of a trilateral meeting. But German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who met Xi last week, told ARD the Chinese leader looked “surprised” when asked about potential Ukraine talks and rejected the idea that China, Russia and the U.S. would discuss Ukraine in a trilateral meeting.

The Chinese foreign ministry told the Financial Times it was “in communication with relevant parties regarding the meeting between the Chinese and Russian heads of state,” without mentioning Trump.

]]> en Poll: Brits want the Democrats to win the midterms https://www.politico.eu/article/brits-want-the-democrats-to-win-the-us-midterms/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:22:07 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9261414 LONDON — Brits would like the Democrats to triumph in the U.S. midterms and believe a Republican win would be riskier for the world, according to a new POLITICO poll.

A survey by pollster PF Global found that 40% of Britons would rather the Democrats win control of Congress in U.S. elections on Tuesday, compared to just 15% preferring the Republicans.

Even among Reform UK supporters — the right-wing party led by Donald Trump ally Nigel Farage — only 27% want a Republican win compared to 21% for the Democrats.

Brits see a Republican hold as a riskier result for the world, with a third expecting global affairs to get more chaotic if the U.S. president’s party controls Congress, compared to 17% who believe it will be less chaotic.

Trump has long been unpopular with the British public, and 55% say his presidency has been bad for the U.K. compared to 17% who think it’s been good. His administration is slightly more popular with Reform supporters — but 38% of that cohort still view it negatively, compared to 27% who regard it positively.

EU is a more ‘reliable ally’

Brits see a raft of other nations and blocs as more reliable partners than the U.S., the PF Global survey suggests. Only 35% trust the U.S. to act as a reliable ally to the U.K. — a far lower figure than for Australia (66%), Canada (65%), Germany (54%), the European Union (53%) and France (50%). Of the seven options given, those surveyed only saw China as a less trusted partner than the U.S.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s push for a closer relationship with the EU appears to also have public support.

The survey suggests more than half the British public (54%) back prioritizing strengthening relations with the EU over Commonwealth countries (46%) and the U.S. (29%).

Burnham traveled to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in the Caribbean on Monday as he seeks to build greater economic cooperation with the 56-strong association of countries — most of which are former territories of the British Empire.

Only Reform supporters put strengthening U.S. relations at the top of their list (52%) compared to 48% for Commonwealth countries and 34% for the EU.

Seb Wride, head of polling at PF Global, said: “President Trump has rapidly reshaped the transatlantic relationship. Brits see their traditional ally as less reliable, and that is pushing them to explore other alliances.

“The question is how far this sentiment extends beyond Trump. A blue wave might be enough for some Brits to feel Trump got what he deserved. But repairing the special relationship is a much bigger ask of a midterm election that few Brits are watching closely.”

Indeed, just 22% said they’ve heard a lot about the midterms, compared to 40% who had heard a lot about England footballer captain Harry Kane winning the prestigious Ballon d’Or trophy for the best-performing footballer.

PF Global polled 2,038 U.K. adults between Oct. 28 and Nov. 2, 2026.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Tue, 03 Nov 2026 21:01:10 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 What Cary, a small town in North Carolina, means for US mid-term elections and everyone else in Europe https://euobserver.com/246525/what-cary-a-small-town-in-north-carolina-means-for-us-mid-term-elections-and-everyone-else-in-europe/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246525 Cary is just a small town in North Carolina. But it is also part of a larger campaign by the Democrats to take over the Senate during this mid-term election.]]> Cary is a small town in North Carolina. Downtown has a library, an Amtrak train station, a beautiful park with a fountain, a post office, an art house cinema, and a single main street with wide sidewalks that divides it in two.

Taipei 101, a Taiwanese takeout on East Chatham Street serves up generous portions of tasty food. I’ve been there myself a few times.

The town is also around a 30-minute drive to the state’s capital city, Raleigh, where former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper is facing Donald Trump’s hand-picked Michael Whatley for a Senate seat in the US mid-term elections.

I first came across Cooper’s name (as a candidate) in March when I saw it posted on somebody’s fence at a stop light in Cary. Some of the pro-Cooper slogans included “Truth over Lies, Hope over Fear”, “Pro-Woman, Pro-Child, Pro-Choice”, and “ICE out for Good”.

Others railing against Trump and his election interference could be seen standing at various street corners in Cary holding up “No King” signs.

]]> Czech public broadcasters hold historic strike following government vote to abolish license fees https://euobserver.com/246573/czech-public-broadcasters-hold-historic-strike-following-government-vote-to-abolish-license-fees/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:56:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246573 Thousand of Czechs joined public TV and radio workers in their walkout over the Czech government's moves to bring public broadcasting under its political control.]]> First published in Deník N.

A strike by workers of public TV and radio workers interrupted broadcasts and drew thousands of people onto the streets across the Czech Republic.

Thousands of protesters gathered in Prague, Brno and Ostrava demonstrations supported by media, students, theatres and more than 300 Czech athletes.

“An unprecedented day in the history of Czech public service media has begun”, said Michal Kubal, Czech Television’s news chief, at 00:00 on 3 November 2026 marking a start to an all-day strike by the broadcasting workers.

He read an opening statement from a sheet of paper during the midnight dispatch. “This broadcast will change. The midnight news is one of many programmes that will look completely different on Czech Television screens from what viewers are used to,” Daniel Stach said on air. The organiser of the strike appeared on TV with a darkened studio as backdrop.

Presenter Kubal went on to explain that staff at Czech Television and Czech Radio were using the one-day strike to fight for independence of both public service media outlets, in response to a government moves to scrap license fees and move public their funding to the state budget.

Read more

Czech government approves first step to scrapping TV and radio licence fees in 4.36am vote, sparking protests

TV management had concluded a memorandum with the strike organisers under which media staff would provide essential news coverage in the event of extraordinary developments.

“A large majority of women and men working at both media outlets have joined the strike. This afternoon, they will also take part in public gatherings in Prague and other cities in support of public service media,” Kubal added.

Those tuning into ČT24 could see a notice about the the public broadcaster’s news network minimalist provisional regime.

“Czech Television employees are on strike. We are doing everything we can to ensure that we can continue providing a public service in full and to the highest standard in the future,” the notice read.

A STEM/MARK survey for Czech Television says 68 percent of people of Czechs agree public service media should stay well away from state control or private ownership.

“Thank you for watching Czech Television — in times of crisis, at historically pivotal moments and on entirely ordinary weekdays,” said Stach, one of the leading figures of the Veřejnoprávně initiative, which called the strike, as he concluded the roughly five-minute midnight news bulletin.

]]> Firefighters from 19 countries protest EU budget cuts in Brussels https://euobserver.com/246651/firefighters-from-19-countries-protest-eu-disaster-budget-cuts-in-brussels/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:20:39 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246651 Around 1,000 firefighters from 19 countries gathered in Brussels Tuesday to demand more equipment, more staff, and adequate healthcare, only weeks before key EU budget negotiations.]]> Around 1,000 firefighters from 19 countries gathered in Brussels on Tuesday (3 November) to demand more equipment, more staff, and adequate healthcare, only weeks before key EU budget negotiations.

With wildfires growing bigger and more often due to climate change, there needs to be more professional firefighters, with modern equipment, to face them, argues the European Federation of Public Service Unions (EPSU), who organised the protest together with various Belgian workers’ organisations.

As of 7 October, 692 419 hectares burnt in wildfires across the EU this year – an area almost as big as the Greek island of Crete – burning some 30 million tonnes of CO2. Southern countries, Portugal, Greece, Italy, and Spain, suffered most. According to the World Health Organisation, wildfires in Europe have increased by 57 percent since 2022.

Read more

Europe’s summer of wildfires puts spotlight on economic cost of climate inaction

On average, wildfires cause some €2.5bn losses across the EU each year.

The protest gathered in front of a conference on civil protection organised by the EU Commission, where crisis management commissioner Hadja Lahbib presented new guidelines on what citizens should prepare for the first days of an emergency.

The firefighters and unions were there to protest the cuts to the next EU budget for disaster management: from over €10bn requested by the commission to just under €7bn proposed by the Irish presidency last month. Yet that would still be double what the 2021-2027 budget had room for.

“I believe that the risk is getting bigger. So yes, it’s necessary to also increase the support,” Tiago da Cunha, president of a municipality in northern Portugal, where the most summer wildfires hit in 2026, told EUobserver.

Read more

Europe’s 2026 wildfires show the cost of ignoring prevention

Stalo Yostili, 43, has been a firefighter in Cyprus for a decade. She said her country does not recognise how dangerous the profession is. She complained of too few staff, which means for an operation that would normally need 15 firefighters, only six are sent, making it more potentially dangerous.

Profession-specific healthcare is also a big topic, Ireneusz Kierzkowski from the Polish firefighter union, told EUobserver. Retired firefighters often have PTSD, and they also develop cancers more often.

Speaking to EUobserver ahead of the US-mid term elections, taking place on Tuesday (3 November), Gardner says foreign relations are widely under the remit of the executive branch.

“Those who are hoping for a big change from this midterm in terms of US policy. You are probably going to be disappointed,” he said.

With two years left in his presidency, the US-mid terms are largely seen as referendum on the Trump administration; spanning everything from high fuel prices, an unpopular war in Iran, corruption, tariffs, healthcare and immigration.

Trump, in his closing speech in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, instead largely spoke about algae blooms and paint jobs and other building projects around Washington DC.

“The pipes now are totally renovated,” he said, in reference to botched efforts to renovate the pool.

Democrats need three more seats to take the House and flip four in the Senate without losing any of their own. All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, compared to 35 of 100 in the Senate.

But a Democrat Congress could potentially embolden Trump to push for an even more radical foreign policy, warned Gardner.

“It often happens in the past when presidents lose control of the House and Senate, they pick up the shiny toy that they have, which is foreign policy, because that’s where they have basically very wide discretion,” he said.

“If the Democrats win both, it becomes even more radical,” he added.

]]> Microsoft cloud in Ireland under fire for hosting Israeli app used to monitor Palestinians in occupied West Bank https://euobserver.com/246599/microsoft-cloud-in-ireland-under-fire-for-hosting-israeli-app-used-to-monitor-palestinians-in-occupied-west-bank/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:49:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246599 Microsoft hosts key software used to monitor movements of Palestinians in the occupied West bank. Some of this is being hosted in Ireland. ]]> Microsoft software plays a key part in running an app used by Israel to control Palestinian mobility in the occupied territories, a new report found. 

Al Munasseq, meaning ‘The Coordinator’ in Arabic, is an app launched by Israel’s Coordination of Government Activities in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (COGAT) unit in 2019 to manage the movement of Palestinians for work, healthcare, prayer, and everyday tasks.

A report published on Tuesday (3 November) by global consumer group Ekō found Microsoft to be hosting key components of Al Munasseq in data centres in Ireland, effectively enabling what is feared to be mass surveillance.

“For Palestinians, Al Munasseq is the gatekeeper to ordinary life. A cancer patient who needs radiotherapy in Jerusalem, a worker who needs to feed his family, a daughter who wants to sit beside her mother in hospital – all of them must ask Israel’s military for a permit to move across their own stolen land, and that permission runs through the Al Munasseq app,” said Ekō senior campaign director, Rewan Al-Haddad.

Read more

EU risks funding Israeli firms which help develop NAZA-type violent tech

“If a Western tech giant can host the machinery powering apartheid in Ireland, inside the EU, and face no consequences, every other company will learn it can do the same,” Al-Haddad told EUobserver. 

Deputy Sinead Gibney, who serves on the Irish parliament’s AI committee, called for an investigation in light of the report findings.

    ]]>         Serbia’s Student List has been inspirational, but the big test will be forming a stable anti-corruption government https://euobserver.com/246552/serbias-student-list-has-been-inspirational-but-the-big-test-will-be-forming-a-stable-anti-corruption-government/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 15:15:05 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246552 The Serbian campaign looked exceptional. I cannot think of many cases of an opposition that was so decentralised and so democratic internally. The closest comparison may be the early German Greens that had a strong Basisdemokratie ["Grassroots Democracy"] out of conviction; or the faceless and fluid democratic movement in Hong Kong ("Be Water") out of necessity. This is inspirational.]]> The ink had hardly dried under articles explaining lessons learned from Péter Magyar’s electoral overthrow of Hungary’s government, when Serbia’s Student List managed to overthrow the semi-authoritarian Aleksandar Vučić.

    Both cases had similarities: long-standing rulers that lied and flaunted their corruption ever more openly; they were ripe for defeat.

    In both cases the opposition avoided strongly partisan positioning and instead focused on state functioning and anti-corruption. 

    Intriguingly, they had almost identical results: 53 percent of the vote for the opposition, 39 percent for the incumbent party. In both cases the opposition showed unity and campaigned across the country and on social media; a well-known ingredient of any campaign to overthrow entrenched authoritarians. 

    Read more

    Serbia’s student protestors win parliamentary majority – setting scene for showdown with Vučić in December’s presidential poll

    In other ways the two cases are strikingly different.

    The Hungarian campaign was focused on Magyar, a consummate politician and former Fidesz member, who knew the incumbent party from the inside.

    In Serbia a collective of students from different universities turned massive mobilisation against the corrupt government into an electoral platform. 

    In Hungary, Magyar dominated his party, in Serbia, the student collective reached decisions democratically, voting on all major points; an extreme contrast between a one-man show and a movement that hardly had any individual faces. 

    What can we learn from these elections?

    First, we should not get fixated on silver bullets. One success story does not mean that the same recipe works elsewhere. Social movements and electoral campaigns are highly complex and contingent on circumstances. No leader like Magyar appeared in Serbia, no massive student initiative developed in Hungary, although both had similar problems of political repression by the ruling party.

    ]]>         Merz, Meloni and the EU: How political attacks on rescue charities are leaving migrants to drown https://euobserver.com/246480/merz-meloni-and-the-eu-how-political-attacks-on-rescue-charities-are-leaving-migrants-to-drown/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 13:47:48 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246480 Berlin, Rome and Brussels have played a role in the decline in an increasingly vital force in the Mediterranean. Search-and-rescue ships have been hampered by legal hurdles and funding cuts, while the central Mediterranean has become a grave for tens of thousands of people.]]> Search-and-rescue NGO efforts to conduct life-saving work in the Mediterranean face continuous derailment by European authorities hoping to stop migrants reaching EU soil – and drowning thousands in the process.

    Since Friedrich Merz took over as German chancellor in May 2025, all funding to national search-and-rescue organisations has stopped. 

    The conservative leader has faced accusations from other EU leaders that the German NGO vessels prevalent across the central Mediterranean’s deadly zone of migrant crossings have acted as a ‘pull factor’, attracting migration to the EU. 

    Current foreign affairs minister Johann Wadephul went so far as to allege that sea rescue organisations are “enabling people-smuggling gangs to carry out their business” in 2023.

    “Of course we know that people don’t travel into the Mediterranean because there are NGOs [there]. They are escaping famine, conflict, violence, some people are even trapped in Libya,” said Sofia [the charity’s workers use first names only], communications coordinator on board German charity SOS Humanity’s mothership.

    Read more

    How the rescue of 28 people from a makeshift dinghy in a stormy Mediterranean unfolded – exposing the lethal reality of EU border policy

    After rescuing 28 people adrift in an overcrowded dinghy last week, the humanitarian NGO has now in total rescued 5,213 people since August 2022. A third of those were children. 

    SOS Humanity were part of a former funding pool that split €2m from Germany’s federal budget for humanitarian aid between search-and-rescue organisations. Despite growing fuel costs, and increasing legal costs from administrative barriers and port detentions by the Italian government, search-and-rescue groups are now dealing with an astronomical gap in their budget. 

    This has also been compounded since Giorgia Meloni’s far-right Italian government came into power in 2022. 

    Rescue charities operating in the central Mediterranean have subsequently been subject to decree 1/2023, requiring them to navigate directly towards the assigned port of safety following a rescue at sea – in other words, preventing more than one rescue operation at a time.

    Italy’s assigned ports are usually days away from where the rescue took place, with the extra navigation due to distant ports causing SOS Humanity to sail an additional 24,745 km and 62 days in 2025 alone. The exacerbated costs of fuel has caused the group to have to severely reduce its operations for 2027.

    Costly ops, and an alarming human cost

    This comes at a time when their work has become more important than ever.

    ]]>         When adults take over youth protests, EU children’s own demands vanish https://euobserver.com/246292/when-adults-take-over-youth-protests-eu-childrens-own-demands-vanish/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:25:18 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246292 As youth protests spread from France to Belgium, Spain, Italy, Greece and Albania, Europe is confronting a stark test of whether under‑18s are treated as political actors in their own right, or merely as props in adult power struggles.]]> France’s lycée students have taken to the streets over shortages of teachers, crumbling buildings, and inequalities that determine educational opportunities and university admissions.

    Yet, as political parties and trade unions joined the protests and students found themselves confronted by riot police, the debate shifted from their demands to their inability to act for themselves.

    In France, adultism has deep roots, reflected in negative stereotypes of young people, their gradual exclusion from public spaces, and the persistent assumption that children are politically innocent and therefore easily manipulated by adults.

    Here lies a democratic paradox: children are expected to develop into politically responsible citizens, but when they start behaving like them, their political agency suddenly becomes questionable.

    Lost in this debate, however, is the fact that students are making political claims of their own, challenging not only their school conditions, but also the political decisions and budgetary priorities that perpetuate these inequalities and jeopardise their future.

    Read more

    Generation Z in France, Spain and Albania is trapped: study hard, stay poor, live with your parents. No wonder they’re protesting

    A right to speak, but who will listen?

    Beyond the political controversy, children are already political citizens, even without voting rights.

    The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, ratified by every state except the United States, guarantees freedoms of expression, association and peaceful assembly, and requires children’s views to be given due weight in matters affecting them.

    The EU and France also have legal provisions recognising children’s participation rights, including in educational governance.

    However, political citizenship extends beyond a formal legal status to participation in public life, where children can actively exercise political agency through expression, collective action, and political claims.

    Their exclusion from electoral politics does not diminish their political legitimacy, nor relieve states of their obligation to take their voices seriously.

    But can blockades and protests bring about the change children demand? Faced with  hundreds of thousands of demonstrators taking to the streets across France in support of students, the French government appears to have rediscovered the virtues of listening to children, launching consultations and promising stronger student representation, more teachers, and funding for school renovations.

    Student representatives welcomed some of these commitments, but insisted on seeing actual renovations and additional teachers in classrooms.

    With the 2027 presidential election approaching in France, these commitments risk becoming entangled in campaigning, and potentially overshadowing children’s demands with competing political agendas.

    The question is what will come of the promises; and just as importantly, who will be held accountable, and how, if those promises are never delivered?

    Read more

    Europe’s youth asked for hope – but politicians just offer fear and hate

    Adults arrive, children disappear?

    The growing involvement of adults (teachers, parents, unions) in the protests also fuelled accusations of political instrumentalisation: the government was quick to accuse left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) of manipulating the children.

    If there was any adult interference, it deserves scrutiny, but assuming that children must be manipulated whenever they organise politically is mere adultism disguised as paternalistic concern. 

    Concerns over the criminalisation of children’s protests have also grown. While incidents of vandalism and violence overshadowed students’ demands, the crackdown was striking: by 14 October, 6,773 minors had been taken into custody, with 2,190 of them facing prosecution.

    Children are apparently mature enough to face legal consequences, even as their political competence is questioned.

    Meanwhile, investigations into police violence against minors raise questions about the state’s duty to protect them.

    As the riots of 17 October erupted into violence and chaos, students’ demands seemed to have faded from sight amid an increasingly heated debate over public order and wider social and political tensions.

    Meanwhile, protests by young people have also taken place elsewhere in Europe, in Belgium, Spain, Italy, Greece, and Albania.

    Although grievances and political circumstances differ, these protests reveal an important distinction between schoolchildren and university students as political citizens.

    Most university students can vote, allowing them to turn collective mobilisation into electoral pressure, as Serbia’s student-backed movement showed when it won the parliamentary election on 25 October.

    But most secondary-school pupils have no equivalent leverage: their political citizenship depends on adults and institutions taking their demands seriously, without constantly calculating how many votes they could win or lose. 

    Beyond the diverse political interpretations of these protests lies another important question: what will children themselves take away from these experiences, and how might these impact their political citizenship?

    They may seek greater influence through consultations, intensify protests or create alternative forms of participation.

    But if their demands continue to fall on deaf ears, while protesting exposes them to the threat of police repression and to adultism, disillusionment may instead drive some away from political participation altogether.

    The promise of children’s rights to be heard was certainly more ambitious than that.

    ]]>         Listen: What’s at stake for Europe in the US midterms? https://euobserver.com/246416/listen-whats-at-stake-for-europe-in-the-us-midterms/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 10:46:54 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246416 Americans are voting today in the midterm elections. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, along with a third of the Senate and according to the polls, the Republicans are expected to lose seats.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below:

    Americans are voting today in the midterm elections. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs, along with a third of the Senate. According to the polls, the Republicans are expected to lose seats.

    What would a Democratic win actually change for Europeans? First, a quick word on what to expect tonight. Polls suggest a win for the Democrats camp, especially in the House of Representatives. 

    It is actually common for the president’s party to lose ground at the midterms. And Donald Trump’s approval ratings have been falling steadily.

    So, if the Democrats do win, what could they do? Quite a lot, on paper at least. Congress holds significant powers. The House can, for instance, launch impeachment proceedings against the president. But removing him from office would require a two-thirds majority in the Senate, which is very hard to reach.

    The Democrats have said they would open investigations into the administration, including on corruption. They want to keep financial support for Ukraine in place, and to end the war in Iran. They also want to roll back many of the tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.

    Read more

    THIS WEEK: EU enlargement report tops Brussels agenda as ‘coalition of the willing’ faces Trump’s midterm test

    These are all issues of great importance for Europe. But could the Democrats really undo them?

    For several of these issues, a simple majority is enough to pass a law. So on that front, they could take a stand. But there is a catch: the president has a veto.

    And to override this veto, Congress needs a two-thirds majority in both chambers. In the House, that means around 290 seats. And even in the most optimistic polls, the Democrats don’t get there.

    Those polls currently point to a tight race for the Senate, and a more comfortable Democratic win in the House.

    Of course, these are estimates to be taken with a pinch of salt. The BBC reminded us yesterday that polls in the United States regularly get it wrong, although they do so less often for midterms.

    Read more

    Trump, Rubio and Hegseth are fumbling Ukraine – Europe needs to stop making the same mistake

    In any case, a two-thirds majority looks like an unlikely scenario. Still, this doesn’t mean nothing will change. The Democrats would still have some levers if they do win.

    They could, for example, block bills by simply refusing to vote for them. And they could hold up the budget, and with it, the funding of the war effort.

    In the case of the tariffs, the Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that Donald Trump had overstepped his powers since Congress had not approved the tariffs. This is already a difficulty, even if, for now, the government is playing with the legal basis of the tariffs. 

    So, to sum up: the Democrats wouldn’t be able to overturn Donald Trump’s policies altogether, but they could make his life a lot harder.

    ]]>         Andrew Tate’s toxic legacy in Romania is warping its democracy https://euobserver.com/246239/andrew-tates-toxic-legacy-in-romania-is-warping-its-democracy/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 09:17:48 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246239 While prosecutors chase the Tates across borders, their macho fantasy of domination is already shaping how a frustrated generation of Romanian men sees women and democracy itself.]]> Prosecutors in Romania officially charged social media influencers Andrew and Christian Tate with trafficking and sex offences involving minors on 4 September. But the Tates were not around to be hauled into a police station in Bucharest – they were in a Miami jail fighting extradition to the UK on similar charges.

    That two of the world’s most high-profile misogynists may finally be brought to justice is a reason to celebrate. But in the country which hosted them for so many years, their toxic legacy continues to pollute the atmosphere.

    Why did the Tates choose Romania in the first place?

    Before his arrest Andrew Tate expressed a preference for countries where “corruption is accessible to everybody.” 

    An underregulated webcam industry and struggles with combating sex trafficking could also be contributing factors.

    But this only partially explains why the self-styled ‘king of toxic masculinity’ may have based himself here since 2017, and why his poisonous messages had fertile ground in which to germinate.

    Once we understand that, we might be able to start pushing back before it’s too late. 

    Read more

    Why AI-turbocharged misogyny and porn are threats to EU democracy

    Compared to other countries in the region, Romania’s feminist movement is relatively young.

    A fertile ground for toxic masculinity

    In 2000, the Romanian edition of Playboy published a supposedly satirical article titled: “How to Beat Your Wife Without Leaving Marks.”

    The outrage prompted the first major waves of protests and women’s rights activism against gender-based violence and its normalisation in Romanian society.

    But in 2026, Romania ranks low in European rankings on gender equality metrics, and high on incidents of domestic violence.

    Romania has no mandatory gender equality education and no comprehensive sex education, while across swathes of the country, boys and young men lack access to quality education and jobs.

    Successive governments have failed to improve their circumstances, and traditional, social pressure on men to provide for a family or partner fosters anger and resentment.

    The manosphere’s appeal

    This disillusioned generation presents ripe pickings for demagogues like the Tates to sell a cartoonish fantasy of success based on subjugating women. 

    Because of lack of any national data, our organisation helped conduct the first nationally representative study into how rapid social and technological advances are reshaping the values, gender perceptions, and political choices of young Romanian men.

    Our findings show a mixed picture where patriarchal beliefs endure but alongside self-confidence issues over how to bond with women.

    While 53 percent strongly agree that “in a relationship, a woman should be available for sex whenever her partner wants it,” a slightly higher percentage believe that women still do not have adequate rights. 

    The dividing lines are not created by age or urban versus rural but by education and economic precariousness.

    A quarter of respondents with university education agree that a man’s honour must be defended through violence, a figure that rises to 50 percent by those with vocational education.

    Whereas formal education covering these issues is absent, the online environment fills the vacuum and the misogynistic, racist, and homophobic values of the manosphere connect to extreme-right movements in Romania and worldwide.

    Our concerns are that the Tates’ legacy on the minds of young people is so damaging that we may only see the true effects in years to come.

    A better model of masculinity

    But it is never too late to act. In April, Romanian parliament overwhelmingly supported a new law defining the concept of femicide with offenders given potential life sentences.

    The legislation also calls for teaching on gender equality and non-violent relationships to be included in the national curriculum, though this is yet to be implemented.

    Many young men are still open to alternative ideas, so we have time to shape their attitudes and we should not delay – 72 percent interviewed agree democracy is a good form of government but 58 percent want a strong leader who does not bother with parliament or elections. 

    As a riposte to the commercial masculinity bootcamps run by manosphere characters, our organisation runs free and healthy masculinity camps for young men between 18 to 22 years old.

    Led mostly by male trainers, participants from across the country and from a broad socioeconomic background discuss their ideas of masculinity, democracy, extremism, and mental health.

    Many describe loneliness, a lack of physical spaces to build friendships, and a growing guilt for being male.

    Providing young men with a non-judgmental environment to open up is a better way to ensure a safer society, rather than putting the onus on women to change their behaviour. 

    Young men also need to be taught media literacy, so they can recognise hate speech and radicalisation techniques used by the manosphere and the far right to target them.

    Positive male role models can encourage young men to open up about problems, but they also need to be exposed to narratives instilling the values of democracy and pluralism.

    Online platforms remain vastly under-regulated, while offline spaces that provide young people, male and female, with environments in which to socialise and form meaningful connections are lacking. 

    Politicians have successfully harvested the Tates’ audience through skilled social-media targeting, and this bore fruit in the last presidential elections, where young men voted heavily for parties headed by authoritarian leaders.

    The radical right is currently leading the polls, and ongoing political deadlock may yet result in them entering government.

    Young Romanian men are not yet a lost cause, but without a concerted societal effort to combat the sinister forces that influence them, democracy in Romania, and across Europe, may not survive their loss.

This comes after several investigations into the agency were launched in recent years.]]> The European Institute of Innovation & Technology (EIT), which received €435m in taxpayer money in 2025, is the only EU agency out of a total of 43 whose accounts did not yield a “clean opinion” in the most-recent audit.

    The accounts of the innovation hub did not properly reflect an €8.7m recovery uncertainty, according to a report by European Court of Auditors (ECA) last week.

    Several dozen of its auditors check the EU agencies every year to form a basis for Brussels bodies to later make decisions on funding.

    The financial audit delivers the latest blow to the EIT, an EU agency whose bodies have faced several investigations over spending.

    “Taxpayers should be concerned,” said Kenneth Haar, researcher at Corporate Europe Observatory, a watchdog. “I find it amazing and worrying to see the EIT house is still not in order, though it was more than two years ago that investigators first stepped in.”

    Lead ECA auditor Petri Sarvamaa said, “The good news is that public money is managed well overall. But the weaknesses we identified also show why strong checks are essential in protecting EU taxpayers’ money.”

    Based in Budapest, the EIT aims to boost European competitiveness by connecting enterprises, researchers and education.

    It distributes funds to sector-specific partnerships called knowledge and innovation communities (KICs). And the spending habits of some of these KICs have caused a financial and reputational headache for EIT bosses.

    Agency disputes €8.7m figure

    The ECA’s report of the EIT’s financial accounts published on Thursday (29 October) said the innovation hub’s grant payments were affected by “a material level of error”.

    But because verification checks were incomplete, it “could not provide an estimated error rate” of grant payments.

    The report also flagged that the agency could fail to recover €8.7m. At least some of this is due to EIT Manufacturing, a KIC which filed for liquidation in March 2026.

    The audit states: “An impairment should have been recognised […] EIT receivables and net assets are overstated by €8.7m, impairment expenses are understated by the same amount, and the economic result for the year is overstated by €8.7m.”

    But the innovation and tech agency disagreed with these findings.

    While the EIT acknowledged that an impairment should have been recognised, it told auditors the amount is actually up to €0.5m, not €8.7m. The chance of recovering the money, the EIT said, is “very likely”.

    Specifically, it expects to recover €5.9m via the so-called Mutual Insurance Mechanism (MIM), and €2.3m by offsetting money owed by EIT Manufacturing.

    The court of auditors also said risks are “amplified” by the use of multiannual grants reported and cleared only every 18 months. In response, the EIT said it is moving to 12-month reporting periods.

    “I think this is all about the pitfalls of letting private actors handle public money, and with relatively few strings attached…. it invites the sort of trouble we have seen,” added Haar.

    “At another level, I believe it is a symptom of the laissez-faire approach of the EU institutions to start-ups and innovation.”

    Read more

    EU’s Horizon-suspension sanction for Israel ‘a bad joke’, says Borrell

    Pumped up KICs?

    EU law sets out that in their seventh year, KICs should be subject to scrutiny before they can receive another seven years of taxpayer money.

    They are envisioned to become financially independent and sustainable after 15 years of existence.

    In 2025, the digital, clean energy, and climate change KICs were due to be independent as they reached their 15th birthdays. 

    But in 2026-27 two of them reportedly received a shared total of €43m from the EIT, which pumped up KICs with EU funds past the supposed expiration date.

First touching land after having survived a sail aboard an overcrowded dinghy in a storm, 28 migrants were trooped through a sped-up "tick-boxing" screening, which experts worry will not accurately measure the vulnerabilities they're up against. ]]> The survivors of a recent maritime migrant rescue operation carried out by the German NGO SOS Humanity were screened on the port docks as they first set foot on EU soil, revealing the insensitive efficiency at the centre of the EU’s new Pact on Migration and Asylum.

    Read more

    How the rescue of 28 people from a makeshift dinghy in a stormy Mediterranean unfolded – exposing the lethal reality of EU border policy

    The reception policies from the pact, implemented in June 2026, require an initial screening of new EU arrivals to last a maximum of seven days. 

    The 28 survivors rescued from an overcrowded dinghy on a stormy night in the central Mediterranean were disembarked at 11 am on Saturday (31 October), and had finished being processed by the evening.

    Under the new pact, that means their asylum decision will have been most likely conducted then and there. 

    The platform alongside the Humanity 1 vessel was bustling with hazmat suits and police. In the northern Italian port of Livorno, a makeshift processing centre was set up to host the Red Cross’s health scan, the EU agency for asylum’s vulnerability scan and legal information session, as well as the police’s interrogation – all to be carried out within hours of migrants’ stunned arrival.

    “Immediately after a rescue, when people only need to rest, they sit through a compressed screening for authorities to rush through a tick-boxing exercise,” said Marta [the NGO requests only first names are used by journalists], SOS Humanity’s protection officer, as survivors from the ship’s rescue were being disembarked by authorities.

    She had prepared vulnerability certificates for those most in need, in the hope their case be treated with more care. 

    “Some border interrogations can become violent, a person has just disembarked and they are suddenly facing hours of interrogations,” Marta told EUobserver. She has often seen armed Frontex or Europol officers standing along the ship at port, towering over migrants in their most vulnerable hours.

    The new pact on migration foresees police registration into Eurodac, a database set up to share information with other member states, followed by an immediate decision as to whether a newcomer should qualify for an accelerated asylum procedure. 

    That means those from nationalities less likely to be granted asylum would receive an answer within 12 weeks, and are most probably going to be rejected.

    “There’s no way you can do an accurate screening of all the traumas someone on this journey has lived in 10 minutes with a police officer,” she added.

    ]]>         Zelensky stalls on his EU promises to protect gay rights, even as Ukraine rushes through minority-languages law https://euobserver.com/245901/zelensky-stalls-on-his-eu-promises-to-protect-gay-rights-even-as-ukraine-rushes-through-minority-languages-law/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 11:05:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245901 Zelensky’s government has shown it can move at lightning speed to please EU partners on some minority rights, yet same-sex partnership and hate-crime bills remain stuck in the Ukrainian parliament.]]> Two months before Kherson was liberated in November 2022, Russian soldiers searched a young shop assistant’s home and found two flags: one Ukrainian, one rainbow.

    In testimony published in July by the United Nations and the Ukrainian rights group Projector, the woman, identified by the pseudonym Olena, described being dragged away, beaten, and threatened with sexual violence. Her captors demanded the names of other LGBTI people in the city. At the time of publication, she had not reported any of this to Ukrainian law enforcement.

    On 12 October, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky signed a national human rights strategy that, for the first time, devoted a section of its own to LGBTI rights. It identifies LGBTI people as a group at heightened risk and commits the state to fighting discrimination and hate crimes. The strategy is tied to Ukraine’s bid to join the European Union. The cabinet has six months to draw up an implementation plan.

    Read more

    Attacks on LGBTI people are the warning sign of a wider backlash against democracy

    I have watched my country make promises like this before. The decree replaces a strategy that Zelensky signed in 2021. The hate crimes bill introduced that year never reached a vote and was withdrawn in 2025. I want to know what will make this promise any different.

    Parliament acted on another question of minority rights that same day. Hungary had blocked two clusters of Ukraine’s accession talks until Kyiv expanded schooling in EU languages for national minorities.

    Those minorities deserve protection. What struck me was how quickly Parliament could provide it. The bill was introduced at the start of October, passed and signed on 12 October. The next day, the EU opened the two clusters.

    Meanwhile, progress on LGBTI rights has been much slower, despite the EU’s equality benchmarks.

    A registered-partnerships bill for same-sex and different-sex couples, introduced in March 2023, has sat in the legal policy committee ever since.

    A bill adding sexual orientation and gender identity to the criminal code’s hate crime provisions has been in committee since August 2025.

    And Ukraine’s own EU roadmap, adopted in May 2025, set the third quarter of that year as the target for passing partnership legislation – the deadline came and went without a vote.

    In February, the Supreme Court let stand a ruling recognising two men as a family, rejecting a challenge from a conservative campaign group. Two months later, Parliament voted 254 to 2 to advance a new Civil Code reserving, de facto, family unions to a man and a woman.

    Rights groups warn that the wording could prevent similar rulings. The speaker has since submitted amendments restoring the current definition of family. Parliament has yet to vote on them.

    When hate crimes become hooliganism

    These failures matter when someone goes to the police to report an attack. In May, after a rally in Ivano-Frankivsk against the Civil Code, men from a “traditional values” counter-event followed the LGBTI activist Olena Shevchenko and a colleague, knocked them down, and stole their posters.

    The police say officers intervened at once and cited two men for petty hooliganism. The women say they spent hours at the station, where officers tried to discourage them from filing and would not record a discriminatory motive.

    In July, someone left severed pigs’ heads and entrails outside a Kyiv branch of a salon chain that had publicly backed LGBTI rights, and poured blood on the steps. The police opened a case for hooliganism.

    Calling an attack hooliganism can leave out why the victim was targeted. The criminal code does not explicitly list sexual orientation or gender identity as hate crime grounds.

    The European Commission also found last year that Ukraine did not systematically collect data on such crimes. In the first half of 2026, Nash Svit, a Ukrainian rights group, documented violations by police in 10 of the 16 cases involving police that it monitored. In one, a gay man in Lviv reported blackmail and threats to out him.

    Police declined to open a case, saying the matter was too small.

    It is Olena’s decision whether to report what happened to her in Kherson. The state owes her a safe way to do so. Its new strategy acknowledges that distrust of public authorities and fear of stigma keep LGBTI people from seeking help. The government is describing people who fear the very institutions they should be able to turn to.

    A strategy without legal recognition

    The strategy also leaves out a specific commitment to legally recognise same-sex partnerships, as the National LGBTI Consortium has pointed out.

    A 2023 judgment of the European Court of Human Rights found the lack of recognition discriminatory. Ukraine is bound by that judgment as a party to the European Convention on Human Rights, and whether or not it joins the EU, accession talks add leverage and a timetable, and Ukraine has already missed the deadline in its own roadmap.

    Read more

    [Interview] Ukrainian MP Ivanna Klympush: ‘I would like to see the countries that joined the EU and had no problems with corruption’

    In July, I wrote in The New York Times about LGBTI soldiers waiting for the state to recognise their partners. Olena was a shop assistant who kept a flag. Nobody should have to become a hero to receive ordinary rights.

    Both bills should go to a vote before the Civil Code’s second reading. The government should fund confidential legal aid outside the big cities and publish how LGBTI complaints are handled, with identities protected. The EU should hold Ukraine to the benchmark it has already written, which names the 2023 judgment.

    Olena’s two flags should never have made her a target. Ukraine cannot undo what Russian soldiers did to her in Kherson, but it can make sure that, if she ever walks into a police station, she gets protection and her complaint is taken seriously. Parliament knows how to turn a commitment into law. It showed as much on 12 October.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/03/small-business-economy-wisconsin-house-race</link>
      <description><p>Affordability and small businesses’ economic woes feature heavily in the House race for Wisconsin’s third district</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-election-results-live-updates">US midterms 2026 live – latest updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/nov/03/midterm-elections-full-results-senate-house-governor-races">Track live results from all 50 states</a></p></li></ul><p>After 18 years in business, Erin Klaus is closing her storefront, a handmade artisan market in downtown Eau Claire, Wisconsin, at the end of the year.</p><p>She opened Tangled Up in Hue amid a recession, during a time when downtown was “kind of a ghost town”, weathering construction and the pandemic. But the current economic crisis proved too much. She’s seen a downward trend in sales for two years, and was dipping into her own pocket from her other job, as the executive director of business non-profit Downtown Eau Claire Inc, to pay staff.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/03/small-business-economy-wisconsin-house-race">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi</link>
      <description><p>A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.</p><p>The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shops</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/02/europe-supermarket-fridges-freezers-who-hacking-why">Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?</a></p></li></ul><p>Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.</p><p>Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/02/supermarket-freezers-across-europe-hit-by-second-suspected-cyber-attack">Continue reading...</a></description>

The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. <![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 04 Nov 2026 00:00:17 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Regulator last year recommended that Government should give RTÉ additional €35m in 2027]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/regulator-last-year-recommended-that-government-should-give-rte-additional-35m-in-2027/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/regulator-last-year-recommended-that-government-should-give-rte-additional-35m-in-2027/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 20:23:09 +0000Ireland’s media regulator recommended that the Government allocate an additional €35 million in funding to RTÉ in 2027, almost double the shortfall that was a source of controversy in last month’s budget.

Coimisiún na Meán (CnaM) recommended that the broadcaster receive a total of €275 million next year to help it hit its voluntary redundancy scheme targets and achieve its goal of commissioning more programming from independent producers.

RTÉ was allocated €240 million in the budget last month, €20 million lower than what was agreed as part of a landmark multiyear deal, unexpectedly freezing its funding at 2026 levels.
