Coul Angel                                       2.10pm               Doncaster

Felcitas e/w                                     2.45pm               Doncaster

Nobody Knows                               3.25pm               Doncaster

Lord Melbourne e/w                     3.25pm               Doncaster

]]> 2474163Bill Esdaile Bill Esdaile City watchdog ‘stands ready’ to act on bank windfall tax Budget leak https://www.cityam.com/city-watchdog-stands-ready-to-act-on-bank-windfall-tax-budget-leak/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:31:18 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474102

The boss of the Financial Conduct Authority has said he is prepared to investigate a potential leak of market-sensitive information that sparked a rally in bank shares hours before John Healey’s maiden Budget. In a letter to the Treasury Committee, Nikhil Rathi vowed to engage with Treasury and Cabinet Office officials over how the details [...]]]>

The boss of the Financial Conduct Authority has said he is prepared to investigate a potential leak of market-sensitive information that sparked a rally in bank shares hours before John Healey’s maiden Budget.

In a letter to the Treasury Committee, Nikhil Rathi vowed to engage with Treasury and Cabinet Office officials over how the details of the Chancellor’s windfall tax on banks ended up in the press, and whether “any unlawful disclosure of inside information may have occurred”.

The watchdog chief wrote that parliamentary scrutiny like select committees and leak inquiries were usually a preferred process for “passing judgment on political discourse and government communications”.

But he added the City’s top regulator may “choose to intervene where that discourse, or poor information handling, impacts markets improperly”.

“We stand ready to consider the specifics of any evidence provided to us by Cabinet Office and HMT to decide what, if any, action it is appropriate for us to take,” he said.

Rathi was responding to a letter that Meg Hillier wrote last week, in which the Treasury Committee chair asked whether an apparent leak of the windfall tax’s severity constituted an “improper release of inside information”.

Shares in high-street lenders surged in the hours leading up to the Budget, after Bloomberg News revealed the heavily trailed banks surcharge would only be temporary and not be as high as some had speculated. Lloyds and Natwest shares climbed as much as four per cent before the levy was formally announced, while Barclays jumped 3.7 per cent.

“This appears to have been more than idle speculation,” Hillier wrote in her initial letter, “and it has implications for relevant securities.”

Reeves Budget sparks Treasury probe

Last year, preparations for Rachel Reeves’ final Budget were plunged into disarray by a wave of leaks and briefings. The then-Chancellor made a speech preparing voters for a manifesto-busting income tax rise – before pulling back from the idea amid pressure from Number 10. Policies including a freezing of income tax thresholds, a levy on electric vehicles and a tourist tax all became public knowledge in the pre-Budget period, and the decision to abort the income tax plans sparked a sharp jump in gilt yields.

The rampant speculation prompted the Treasury to launch an inquiry into the leaks. Minister James Murray said the probe, which reported in February this year, would investigate the “security processes to inform future fiscal events”.

In a parallel letter to Treasury permanent secretary James Bowler, Hillier said it would be “deeply concerning” if the leaks were unauthorised given government efforts to tighten Budget security.

She also asked Bowler to confirm that neither banks – nor their trade bodies – were told of the changes “in outline or with specifics” before the Budget, and to reveal how many people had prior access to the policy’s final structure. The Treasury has not responded to the committee’s letter.

]]> 2474102Ali Lyon Ali Lyon Barclays and HSBC bankers donate over $500k in US midterms https://www.cityam.com/barclays-and-hsbc-bankers-donate-over-500k-in-us-midterms/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:29:47 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474140

Barclays and HSBC bankers donated over half a million dollars to US political candidates ahead of the midterm elections. Bankers who are employed at the two UK-headquartered giants flooded cash into US political figures as  millions of Americans headed to the polls. Donors listing Barclays or one of its subsidiaries as an employer contributed just [...]]]>

Barclays and HSBC bankers donated over half a million dollars to US political candidates ahead of the midterm elections.

Bankers who are employed at the two UK-headquartered giants flooded cash into US political figures as  millions of Americans headed to the polls.

Donors listing Barclays or one of its subsidiaries as an employer contributed just over $344k (£256k) to candidates since the beginning of 2025, according to Federal Election Commission figures. 

Chief among those was a whopping $70k from the investment bank’s banking chairman Alexander Lynch, whose sum was sent to the House Victory Project, a fund split across Democrat candidates.

HSBC staff donated over $163k, according to FEC data. This was led by Mark Schuermann, head of public affairs in the US, who donated around $18k with $8k going to the bank’s Political Action Committee (PAC).

The group has different PACs which are financed by voluntary employee donations. This pooled money is kept separately and is isolated from company profits to comply with campaign laws. 

A HSBC spokesperson said: “HSBC Political Action Committees are committees formed by eligible employees and they are not controlled by HSBC nor use HSBC funds.”

They added the committees operate in a “bipartisan manner contributing to candidates of all political parties” and seek to ensure “an even split between parties”.

The bank focuses its US operations on international commercial banking, wealth management, and wholesale markets. It has major coastal hubs like New York, San Francisco and Miami.

US gears up for ‘referendum on Trump’

Of the big four UK banks, Barclays and HSBC have the greatest presence in the US. Individuals listing Natwest and Lloyds Banking Group as their employers donated around $5k collectively.

Barclays operates a major investment banking and corporate presence based out of New York. It also has a targeted consumer business focused primarily on co-branded credit cards with American airlines and retailers. 

A Barclays spokesperson said the bank is a “politically neutral organisation and does not engage in party political campaigning or make party political donations”.

They added that colleagues involved in political activity in a personal capacity have “a responsibility to make sure that this is kept entirely separate from their duties as an employee” and that Barclays’ funds are not used for political purposes.

The US midterms will contest all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 out of the 100 in the US senate. 

It is broadly expected to be fought on issues around the economy with many pollsters viewing the elections as a referendum on Donald Trump.

US inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent in September 2026, above market expectations and up from 3.4 per cent in each of the previous two months.

]]> 2474140Samuel Norman Samuel Norman Asda’s turnaround king names heir to the throne https://www.cityam.com/asdas-turnaround-king-names-heir-to-the-throne/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 16:19:37 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474176

Allan Leighton was adamant. Just two months ago, Asda’s then-executive chairman insisted that his position as the sole leader of the discount grocer’s turnaround plans would not change any time soon.  It had been rumoured that Asda was on the lookout for a chief executive to bolster its efforts to return to its heyday, but [...]]]>

Allan Leighton was adamant. Just two months ago, Asda’s then-executive chairman insisted that his position as the sole leader of the discount grocer’s turnaround plans would not change any time soon. 

It had been rumoured that Asda was on the lookout for a chief executive to bolster its efforts to return to its heyday, but Leighton told City AM that any changes of leadership were “not imminent”. 

And when any change of leadership finally arrived, he said, it would come from within Asda’s existing top team. “The preference would be to appoint a CEO from inside the company, and we have a very highly talented group of executives, and my hope is that somebody would emerge from the group,” he had said. 

Just weeks later Leighton has already handed over the top job – to an outsider. David Potts, a former boss of rival Morrisons, took the reins as chief executive role with immediate effect, prompting Leighton to step back into a non-executive chairman position. 

This apparent U-turn was “unexpected but not entirely surprising,” independent retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth said. Asda has been searching on-and-off for a chief executive since the departure of Roger Burnley in 2021. 

Petrol station tycoon Mohsin Issa, who bought the grocer from US retail giant Walmart for £6.8bn in 2021, was Asda’s boss until September 2024 but the group has been without a chief executive since Leighton’s appointment as executive chairman. 

While Leighton said he was looking inwards to find his successor after exhausting his external search, the Asda chairman told the Times that he had been pursuing Potts all along.

Football is embracing technology. Computers and screens are being used to give or strike off goals; data is now firmly embedded in player analysis – in a move that has helped the likes of Brighton and Hove Albion and Hearts – and now Bundesliga side TSG 1899 Hoffenheim are using AI to help in their deadline day recruitment and matchday preparation.

“We think about game preparation through a quicker search for clips, different patterns which are then used to really understand the opponent’s movements or patterns,” Gross tells City AM. “Especially for this game, the preparation is still running but it’s in the end phase so we’re ready to get this game running.”

While its main market continues to be the German top flight, SAP’s sport strategy lead Fadi Naoum says that the firm’s Sports One system has undisclosed customers in the Premier League and was used by some national teams at this year’s men’s World Cup. 

But is there a risk of the AI going solo and modelling itself based on rival data? Could one club use its systems as if it was its opponent and unlock an advantage? The answer is rather boring, if not reassuring, sadly.

“We are very strict when it comes to the GDPR, security and privacy,” Naoum says. “Why all the Bundesliga and our customers trust us is because we have for every club its own system – there is no cross-data, it’s up to the club what kind of data you feed the system.”

The growing use of technology in sport has some fans worried, and Gross admits that AI “will change the whole landscape of job profiles” at Hoffenheim and beyond. He talks through a scenario whereby the SAP technology is used during a transfer window to identify potential signings, injury replacements and to do last-minute reconnaissance on a player who has arrived into the transfer mix close to the deadline.

Their use of AI not only allows for the analysis of player patterns – shots, dribbles, chances taken and the like – but behaviours too. “You can think about body language, data points which weren’t there but now you have it as a side product,” Gross adds. But it won’t see human scouts replaced entirely.

“The data is then connected to an action to give actionable insight,” Gross, who joined Hoffenheim as an intern in 2013, says.

“This is where the validation process with a human being is also in place, but with the help of AI, everything is more efficient and more to a level that we have questions to ask which we didn’t before.”

Pension providers have questioned whether the government can deliver on its plans to guarantee retirement income for millions of private sector workers.

Pensions minister Torsten Bell unveiled plans on Tuesday which will require pension providers to offer workers an annual income as standard in retirement.

Dubbed ‘Guided Retirement’, the overhaul is anticipated to bring private sector retirement savings closer to that of public workers, who typically have Defined Benefit schemes.

DB schemes guarantee employees a regular, lifetime income upon retirement calculated by length of employment and salary. 

This differs to private defined contribution (DC) schemes where a worker’s retirement fund is built entirely from money paid by them, their employer and tax relief, which creates the risk of people not having enough money upon entering retirement.

While pension providers have welcomed the possibility of improved retirement savings and the removal of having to deal with difficult financial decisions, some questioned the loss of choice.

Ending flexibility

“Default retirement solutions can help, particularly for those who don’t want to navigate complex decisions themselves. But they should be a safety net rather than a straitjacket,” said Jon Greer, head of retirement policy at Quilter.

“People must retain the flexibility to choose a different approach and access personalised advice where appropriate.”

Emma Furlonger, managing director and retail intermediary at Standard Life, added that a default should provide a “guardrail” rather than being shoehorned in as a “substitute”.

“People should understand the approach being offered, have meaningful opportunities to consider whether it remains right for them and retain the freedom to choose an alternative,” she said.

Income guaranteed?

While the government’s plans lean heavily on “resurrecting proper pensions” for the private sector, providers have pointed out limits to this possibility.

The Retirement Collective pension schemes put forward as an option by Bell to create guaranteed income are hybrid arrangements which combine elements of both DC and DB schemes. 

Instead of individual pots, employers and employees make fixed-percentage contributions into a shared fund managed by trustees.

Laura Mason, chief executive of retail at Legal & General said they can be a “valuable part of the landscape”, but that “higher expected income isn’t free”.

“[The scheme] involves investment risk, and unlike an annuity, income isn’t guaranteed,” she said.

It does not legally guarantee a pension income and the amount received can fluctuate if the pooled fund underperforms or life expectancy rises.

Ken Scott, lead actuary at Royal London, said: “A guaranteed income for life and a guaranteed level of income aren’t necessarily the same thing… the detail of the Government’s proposals will be important.”

Blurred lines and demand

Other providers urged the government to ensure “strong alignment” between the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) and Pensions Regulator, arguing a fragmented regime will prevent the overhaul being implemented effectively.

The UK DC market is currently split between trust-based schemes overseen by the Pensions Regulator under DWP legislation and contract-based schemes which are regulated directly by the FCA.

“It is important that the new framework aligns with the wider policy landscape,” said James Carter, head of platform policy at Fidelity International.

“This is a pivotal policy and there remain some important principles to be settled to ensure pension members are best supported.”

Despite the overarching positive reaction from the pensions industry, delivering the changes will heavily rely on their systems which could cause heavy operational strain.

Maurice Titley, commercial director of data and dashboard at Lumera, said: “Delivering this will place considerable demands on providers’ data, technology and governance capabilities.

“They will need to understand their membership, identify appropriate cohorts, support transitions between different phases of retirement and demonstrate that the outcomes being delivered match those expected.”

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) confirmed on Tuesday that vulnerable refrigeration technology had been exploited in a small number of incidents in Britain, after hackers remotely manipulated supermarket fridge temperatures across several European countries.

The attacks have forced retailers in Sweden, Belgium, Ireland and elsewhere to throw away large quantities of fresh and frozen food after refrigeration systems were switched into defrost mode.

Richard Horne, chief executive of the NCSC, said the agency had “worked through the night” to warn potentially affected British businesses.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Horne said it was too early to identify those responsible.

“It’s too early for us to say at the moment and give a definitive answer”, he said.

When asked whether the incidents reinforced warnings from the Defence Secretary that Brits should stockpile supplies, Horne replied: “Absolutely. And we saw criminal attacks last year impact retailers in the UK”.

“We know it can happen, and we’ve seen it across Europe”, he added, warning that years of underinvestment had left the technology underpinning essential services vulnerable.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers, which represents more than 300 businesses, confirmed that some members had been affected, although none had lost any inventory.

The incidents follow a similar attack on hundreds of French supermarkets last month, which caused millions of euros in damage after hackers exploited vulnerabilities in remotely managed fridges.

GCHQ warns of AI-driven cyber threat

The attacks come as Britain’s cyber security chief prepares to warn that AI could trigger an unprecedented increase in cyber incidents by making existing vulnerabilities easier to exploit.

In a speech launching the NCSC’s latest report on Tuesday, Horne described the coming months as a critical turning point for Britain’s cyber defences.

“In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents”, he said.

“But we must be clear that is not because AI has invented new ways to attack us, but because vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long can now be discovered and exploited at a scale that was once unimaginable”.

Cyber security researchers have identified more than 800 fridge interfaces associated with British retailers that are accessible over the public internet.

While that does not necessarily mean the systems can be hacked, experts warn that outdated software and poorly secured remote access can leave critical equipment vulnerable.

Martin Riley, chief technology officer at cyber security firm Bridewell, said the food industry was particularly exposed because its products were perishable and operations depended on tightly controlled temperatures.

“A supermarket fridge holds no secrets. It holds a temperature. Change that temperature overnight and you destroy the value of everything inside it within hours,” he said. “There is no backup to restore from. The stock is simply gone.”

Riley said his firm’s research had identified more than 6,000 refrigeration management panels from a single manufacturer exposed online worldwide.

He warned that attackers were increasingly targeting operational technology, the systems controlling physical equipment, rather than simply stealing data or locking businesses out of their IT networks.

Fears over food security

The incidents have raised concerns about the wider consequences of cyberattacks on essential infrastructure, particularly as supermarkets increasingly rely on internet-connected equipment and third-party contractors.

“The cyberattacks affecting supermarkets across the UK and Europe show how incidents can quickly extend beyond IT disruption, affecting food supplies, businesses and consumers,” said Charl van der Walt, global head of security research at Orange Cyberdefense.

“As in the French refrigerator case, the perpetrators and their motives remain unclear, as does whether the incidents are connected”.

He added that attacks did not need to be deliberately designed to spread fear to have that effect.

“When attackers remain hidden, technical details are difficult to verify and the public is left uncertain, trust can quickly erode.”

Ed Hayes, data protection partner at law firm TLT, said operational technology had historically been a “cybersecurity blind-spot”, with retailers investing more heavily in protecting payment systems and customer data than refrigeration and logistics equipment.

“Legacy OT systems that were never designed with cyber resilience in mind are frequently still in use, running without basic security controls,” he said.

The latest incidents come after cyberattacks on Marks & Spencer and the Co-op last year disrupted deliveries and left supermarket shelves empty.

The British Retail Consortium said retailers were working with the NCSC to strengthen their defences against similar attacks.

The NCSC has not identified who is responsible for the latest incidents, with Horne saying it remains “too early to say” who was behind them.

Instead, chefs and restaurateurs looked at how to raise standards across the workplace, and how to shake hospitality’s very real image problem. 

The event was put on by Verifair, which has just come out with its biennial report on working conditions in hospitality. And some of the figures are hard to swallow. I’ve experienced the Wild West of hospitality firsthand, and the conditions that turn the screw: the long hours and intense pressure. But also blurred lines between work and social life in a boozy industry that is hard to switch off from. Still, Verifair’s finding that over half (52 per cent) of respondents had experienced inappropriate, unsafe or unacceptable behaviour in the last 12 months is not a good look for the sector.

When Justine Murphy set up Verifair to tackle the problems, she did so as an insider. Having spent over 30 years working in the industry, she got to know the cracks and crevices talented workers fall into – and struggle to get out of.

“I love hospitality, but I’ve seen how much someone’s experience really does depend on who they work for. And there are some incredible, exceptional employers, but there’s also people who are experiencing treatment that should just never be accepted. So I really wanted to make responsible employers visible, and create ongoing accountability around how people are treated,” Murphy tells me.

Verifair is a body that assesses restaurants, creating a reference point for employees. To put it simply, is this a good place to work? It’s an enormous undertaking, but Murphy envisages a world where restaurants will display their Verifair plaque alongside Michelin stars. Recently Gareth Ward of double-starred Ynyshir posted a video to social media of him proudly drilling his Verifair qualification badge into a tree alongside years of Michelin awards.

“I think every business that signs up and goes through that process, like Gareth Ward, that’s another person, another voice that’s being lent. And that’s how we slowly but surely will start raising the bar and raising the standard and giving people something to work towards. And that’s how we make positive change,” Murphy says.

The web-like quality of hospitality – one that tips into codependency – is what Murphy built Verifair on, and it’s what will ultimately determine its success going forward. 

“I’ve built really great relationships with people, but I also have carved out a reputation for when I say I’m going to do something, I do it.” And Murphy has the backing to prove it. On her advisory board are some cheffing heavy hitters, including Ikoyi’s Jeremy Chan, West London restaurateur du jour Chris D’Sylva, and Teal’s Sally Abé, who has been especially vocal in raising the standards in kitchens.

I ask Abé about her experiences moulding a career in hospitality: “The biggest thing for me is the idea that fear gets the best out of people. I’ve worked in kitchens where making a mistake meant being screamed at or humiliated in front of everyone. You end up being more worried about the reaction than about fixing the problem.”

She says that loving hospitality means being honest about its shortcomings.

“For a long time, bad behaviour was excused if the chef was talented enough or the restaurant was successful enough. People would say, ‘That’s just what they’re like’, and everyone else was expected to work around it. Murphy wants Verifair to change how we perceive the whole industry, and to do that, the right people need to be in the right positions. As she puts it, “we haven’t got a staffing issue. We’ve got a how people are being looked after issue.”

Whether the system will keep an industry that eschews the norms of a nine-to-five in check is yet to be seen. It’s early days, but when chefs and restaurateurs from across the industry meet in two years’ time for Verifair’s next report, there is tentative hope things can be better. And Murphy has put herself at the heart of that mission.

“Responsible employers deserve recognition, and their people deserve a voice.”

The claim is being brought by the player union Professional Footballers Australia against governing body Football Australia and has reached the New South Wales Supreme Court.

The row has implications for the earnings of several Australian players based in English football, including Norwich forward Mohamed Toure, Swansea defender Cameron Burgess and Arsenal Women pair Caitlin Foord and Steph Catley.

What Football Australia said about the pay row

A Football Australia spokesperson sought to downplay the dispute, saying: “The Supreme Court’s role is limited to the subpoena process, and its involvement ends once that process is complete.” 

The governing body acknowledged that the row was being considered by the National Dispute Resolution Chamber and, as such, is “subject to confidentiality obligations” that prevented FA from commenting further.

The Socceroos reached the last 32 of this year’s men’s World Cup, while the Matildas’ most recent major tournament result was runners-up in the Women’s Asian Cup.

There have been a series of papers published recently that showed that large language models have their own biases when making investment recommendations.

I have previously written about the kind of biases displayed, while this study has looked at the particular biases of different commonly used models.

Fair enough, but what if I tell you that one can manipulate the investment bias of an open-weight LLM by changing a single neuron in the neural network?

That is the concerning message of a new paper by a group of researchers from South Korea and the US.

They started with popular open-weight models (Qwen3, Llama 4, DeepSeek R1, Gemma 4, and Mistral Small) and identified a single neuron in each of these models that would influence the investment bias of the model output.

By changing the activation of this single neuron in the one-weight model, they could switch the investment recommendation for single stocks or entire portfolios without modifying the prompt or updating model parameters!

This is really troubling because it means that every LLM has biases, and advisers using these models will give biased advice that has nothing to do with the investor’s own preferences.

In a closed-weight model like the frontier models, advisers can’t change the activation parameter but also don’t know what the model bias is.

Meanwhile, in an open-weight model, the activation parameter can be identified and manipulated, but that just means that the model then has the investment bias that the adviser wants it to have.

Joachim Klement is an investment strategist and ESG specialist within the strategy team at Panmure Liberum.

Private sector workers are set to be given access to guaranteed pension income for life, as the government aims to close the retirement savings gap between the public and private sector.

Under new plans set out by pensions minister Torsten Bell on Tuesday, providers will be required to offer workers an annual income as standard in retirement.

The plans, dubbed ‘Guided Retirement’, will “resurrect” the option of having an inflation protected pension that provides a secure income for private sector retirees.

Roughly 17m workers who are saving into a default pension will be given the option.

DB guarantee

The move is anticipated to bring retirement savings in the private sector closer to that of the public, where workers typically have a defined benefit (DB) pension.

DB schemes guarantee employees a regular, lifetime income upon retirement calculated by length of employment and salary. This differs to private defined contribution (DC) schemes where a worker’s retirement fund is built entirely from money paid by them, their employer and tax relief.

But over the last 30 years, the vast majority of private DB schemes that once provided an inflation protected income have been shut down.

While the introduction of automatic enrolment in 2012 has boosted saving among private workers, the majority of the UK sector are saving into DC schemes, leaving them without automatic financial security in later life.

“Private sector workers deserve a much better deal when it comes to pensions. They are doing the right thing and saving for retirement, but when they get there too many are left without a genuine pension,” said Bell.

“We are resurrecting proper pensions for private sector workers…and in many cases protection against the rising cost of living. Things public sector workers take for granted.”

Financial knowledge and loss of choice

The plan is also designed to stop savers from having to become “investment experts overnight” as most take control of their pot with little financial knowledge which can cause them to make rushed decisions.

According to the Department of Work and Pensions (DWP), around 46 per cent of first-time pension pot accesses involved a pot being fully withdrawn in the 2025/26 tax years, leaving many facing the risk of entering retirement without sufficient funds or being reliant on the state pension.

But Steve Webb, pensions consultant at LCP and former pensions minister under the Coalition government, warned that pensioners lose the “freedom and choice” of how and where to invest that comes with DB schemes.

“The government is right to say that managing a DC pot in retirement through the ups and downs of markets, and with no idea how long the pot needs to last, is challenging.  But there is a danger that the government’s hostility to pension freedoms will lead them to promote ‘lifetime income’ solutions too heavily,” said Webb.

“Many people will have a good level of secure income… and may prefer the flexibility to take their DC pot in ‘chunks’ as needed, rather than spread thinly through the decades of retirement. It is vital that the focus on retirement income does not destroy ‘freedom and choice’ in pensions which have been popular with savers and given valuable flexibility to hundreds of thousands of people in the last decade.”

Virgin Media O2 has confirmed plans to slash thousands of jobs in the UK under a push to cut its cost base by around £800m, as it grapples with firmer competition and “paradoxical” regulation in the fibre market.

The telecoms giant said around £300m of the total savings would come from cutting its 16,000-strong workforce in the UK, with aims to reduce its staff costs by around 30 per cent by 2029.

The company has not disclosed how many jobs in total will be lost.

The cuts form part of a wider cost-saving drive as Virgin Media O2 seeks to simplify its management structure and reduce spending on contractors and suppliers.

Erhan Gurses, telecoms analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, estimated that the redundancies could generate around £200m in annual gross personnel savings by 2028, with further reductions in contractor spending potentially increasing that figure.

However, he warned that the savings would do little to resolve the company’s balance-sheet pressures, with net leverage potentially remaining close to 5.5 times earnings in 2028, above its target range of four to five times.

“The scale and timing show the cost-saving push has accelerated notably”, Gurses said.

Revenue falls as broadband market shrinks

The restructuring comes as Virgin Media O2 faces pressure from tighter fibre regulation, competition from cheaper broadband rivals and a shrinking market.

In its third-quarter results, the company said service revenue fell 3.5 per cent in the three months to the end of September, with another 23,300 fixed line customer losses on a net basis. It said this was 9,400 fewer than a year earlier.

Overall underlying earnings fell 2.6 per cent in the third quarter as a 5.4 per cent drop in costs failed to offset the service revenue hit.

In a statement, the company said senior leadership changes were “already underway” as part of plans to reduce its “organisational layers”.

“Given the market conditions we face, the regulatory backdrop in fibre and the technological changes sweeping across all areas of the economy, standing still and doing what we’ve always done is not an option and while many of these decisions are tough, they are necessary for our future success and growth,” said Lutz Schuler, chief executive Virgin Media O2.

The company said it had no plans to close any of its UK offices, including sites in London, Reading, Leeds, Manchester and Glasgow.

The company added that the decision came against comes against a backdrop of “a tough macro-economic climate, an intensely competitive and shrinking broadband market and a paradoxical regulatory direction in fibre that does not reflect economic reality”.

Virgin Media O2 said it had no plans to close any of its UK offices, which include sites in Paddington in London, Reading, Leeds, Manchester and Glasgow.

Fibre competition adds pressure

Virgin Media O2, jointly owned by Liberty Global and Telefónica, has also been reviewing its fibre investment strategy as competition intensifies.

The company is understood to be nearing an agreement to use BT’s Openreach network, potentially allowing it to expand coverage without shouldering the full cost of building new infrastructure.

The talks come despite tensions between the two operators, with Virgin Media O2 recently describing BT’s agreed takeover of TalkTalk as a “stitch-up”.

Meanwhile, the Competition and Markets Authority has provisionally raised concerns over nexfibre’s proposed £2bn acquisition of Netomnia. Nexfibre is backed by Virgin Media O2’s shareholders.

The regulator is expected to issue its final decision in December.

Virgin Media O2 said its restructuring reflected a “tough macro-economic climate, an intensely competitive and shrinking broadband market” and a regulatory approach to fibre that it argued failed to reflect economic realities.

Barclays will begin offering payouts to motor finance consumers ahead of the forthcoming legal battle after the City watchdog introduced its “minimum expectations” for lenders wishing to settle early.

The bank said it would make payments using the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) redress scheme methodology and acceptance would be optional. Once a consumer accepts the settlement, they cannot subsequently seek additional compensation.

It comes after the FCA said it would begin to release the names of lenders making payouts before the case heads to the Upper Tribunal in February 2027.

“The regulator supports lenders making settlement offers, as long as customers are offered no less than they would receive through the scheme,” the FCA said.

It added lenders would not be able to claim or imply that the regulator vetted or endorsed their specific cash offer and it must be no less than the maximum redress consumers would have received under the original redress.

Under FCA rules, maximum payouts are calculated per agreement and capped at either a full commission refund or the total financing charges paid, plus statutory interest.

“Lenders have been considering making early settlement offers but have been reluctant to move ahead without a clear signal from the regulator. With that reassurance now in place, we could see a number of lenders break cover and begin offering compensation ahead of the wider scheme,” Harry Charalambous, principal at consultancy Broadstone, said.

FCA’s £9bn redress faces backlash

The watchdog is set to defend its redress scheme against three challenges from the industry and one from advocacy group Consumer Voice.

The FCA published its finalised proposals at the end of March, where lenders were put on the hook for £9.1bn, lower than previously expected, after the number of qualifying agreements was reduced to 12.1m from 14.2m. But fierce backlash across the aisle led to its suspension in July.

The Supreme Court partially overturned a landmark ruling on car finance deals last year, rejecting claims that hidden commissions were automatically unlawful. It found one customer’s undisclosed commission created an “unfair relationship”, leaving the door open for an industry-wide redress scheme by the FCA. 

Volkswagen Financial Services, which has set aside £725m for expected expenses, is among the challengers to the scheme as well as Mercedes-Benz and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance.

Many of the City’s top banks have criticised the scheme but chose not to challenge it in the courts. Lloyds Banking Group – which has set aside £2bn in payouts – said whilst it was “disappointed” it would not challenge the scheme.

Barclays has set aside a total £430m provision bill for compensation through its Barclays Partner Finance arm.

A Barclays Partner Finance spokesperson said: “We recognise that some customers have already faced a considerable wait for an outcome on their motor finance complaints.

“By making these early settlement offers, we are giving some customers the option of receiving redress sooner, rather than waiting for the legal challenges and any subsequent FCA action to conclude.”

Stephen Braviner Roman, the FCA’s general counsel and co-lead on the motor finance project, said:  “Fair settlement offers could result in some people getting money sooner. And it’s clear they want the choice.  

“Anyone who wants to wait can, and there’s no obligation to agree to the offer. We’ll closely monitor firms making offers and expect them to be clear what accepting an offer means.”

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

The way the question is asked

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

A few minutes of small talk

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Across the study, buyers rated their seller’s likely honesty at 6.56 on a ten-point scale, while coders scored the sellers’ actual replies at 7.51. Among pairs who chatted first, that difference was no longer statistically significant. Sellers’ scores did not differ significantly between the two conditions. The chat raised buyers’ expectations of honesty instead.

Study 4 tried a different nudge on 358 participants. Some buyers were asked about the seller’s moral concerns before predicting, others afterward. Thinking about the seller’s conscience first raised buyers’ expectations, and the gap was nearly halved.

It did not close. The authors suggest one reason: 85 percent of sellers in that study disclosed, a rate higher than in the matching condition of Study 3 for reasons they say are not readily apparent.

Where the suspicion comes from

Study 2 measured three motives, adding the pull of money to the two that Study 1 had tracked. The 214 management undergraduates who took part rated, on a seven-point scale, how much the seller had been weighing being decent, feeling guilty, and getting the best price. Sellers put their concern with being a decent person at 4.99, and buyers guessed 3.78. Buyers put the seller’s interest in money at 6.03; sellers reported 5.06.

The sellers still cared about the money. They cared about it less, and about their own decency more, than the buyers pictured.

The paper’s explanation leans on moral typecasting, the idea that people tend to see others as either doers or feelers, rarely both. A seller holds the object and the information, so, the authors argue, a buyer casts them as a doer, and the competitive setting makes that doer look like someone chasing an advantage rather than guarding a clean conscience. In the abstract’s words: “While sellers tended to be honest because of moral identity concerns, buyers expected them to be driven primarily by self-interest.”

Two duller explanations get a hearing too, and the authors say their own mechanism is not the only one. Poor forecasting in general, they point out, gives no reason to expect guesses to run low rather than high. Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.

]]> Quote of the day: “Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself” https://siliconcanals.com/d-quote-of-the-day-sometimes-you-find-yourself-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-and-sometimes-in-the-middle-of-nowhere-you-find-yourself/ Thu, 17 Sep 2026 10:45:39 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109380

What happens when your plans collapse, your phone dies, and you're stranded at a gas station thousands of miles from home—and it's the best thing that could've happened.]]>

The last time I was properly lost, I was standing at a petrol station somewhere north of Chiang Rai with a dead phone, a warm bottle of water and a dog who clearly ran the place. My bus had left without me. I had four hours to wait, nothing to do and no way to tell anyone about it.

It was the calmest I had been in about eighteen months.

Sometimes you find yourself in the middle of nowhere, and sometimes, in the middle of nowhere, you find yourself.

Yes, it is the sort of line that ends up engraved on a bracelet and screwed to somebody’s kitchen wall. Both of which have happened, it turns out. I went looking for whoever wrote it and found nothing, only evidence that it has been circulating since at least 2014 with no author attached. Anonymous, then. It holds up better than most things sold at a craft market.

Nowhere is mostly an absence of audience

Here is what I think the line is really about. Nowhere has very little to do with distance. It is any situation where nobody knows your job title.

In a city you are surrounded by people who already have a version of you loaded. The neighbour who thinks you are the loud one. The old colleague who still introduces you by the thing you did in 2019. You end up performing that version without noticing, because it is easier than correcting everybody.

Take the audience away and something odd happens. For a day or two you feel faintly useless, because nobody needs anything from you. Then the noise drops. You start hearing your own opinions, which are less impressive and a good deal more honest than the ones you say out loud.

That is the whole mechanism. No mysticism required.

The year my diary went blank

I lost my business, restaurants, during the pandemic. The deal was agreed over a phone call while I sat on a plastic chair in a dining room with the lights off, and it was the least bad option available to me at the time.

For years my day had been decided for me by suppliers, staff rotas and the seven o’clock rush. Then it was not. I woke up on a Tuesday with an empty calendar and genuinely no idea what a Tuesday was for.

I would love to tell you this was peaceful. I reorganised the same cupboard twice. I developed strong opinions about a neighbour’s parking. I rang people I had not spoken to in five years and could hear them wondering what I wanted.

The useful part arrived about three months in, once I had run out of things to tidy. With no restaurant to point at, I had to work out what I would actually do with a day if nobody was paying me for it. The answer was writing, which was inconvenient, as it pays considerably worse than a burger.

You can get lost for the price of a bus ticket

You do not need to sell a business or fly to Patagonia. Nowhere comes in small doses and most of them are free.

Pick a district of your own city you have no reason to visit and spend three hours there on foot. Not a famous one. A dull one, with hardware shops and a wet market and nothing on sale to anyone carrying a suitcase. I do this in Bangkok about once a month and I have never regretted it, though I have frequently regretted the shoes.

Go somewhere your phone cannot help you. Not switched off, just outgunned: the lanes are not on the map and the only language on offer is one you do not speak.

Be a beginner at something in public. Take a class where you are visibly the worst person in the room. It is physically uncomfortable for about twenty minutes. After that it stops mattering, and what is left is quite close to fun.

And if you do travel, leave one day entirely unplanned. No booking, no list, no reservation you have to walk fast to reach. Most people schedule a trip so tightly that they never get further than a warmer version of their normal week.

What actually turns up

Let me manage expectations. You do not come back from a petrol station with a revelation.

What you come back with is a shorter list. Two or three things you thought you cared about turn out to belong to somebody else. One or two things you have never mentioned to anyone are suddenly all you think about when there is nothing else to think about. That is it. It looks like very little on paper. It does not feel that way at thirty-eight, when you are still doing a job you picked at twenty-two to impress someone who stopped watching years ago.

There is a trap in this, though. Some people use the middle of nowhere as somewhere to hide, and the giveaway is that they keep having to go back. If every trip is an escape from the same unaddressed thing at home, the scenery is doing the work of a conversation you have been avoiding. Distance is excellent for seeing a problem clearly. It has never once solved one for me.

The dog at the petrol station, for the record, took no interest in any of this. He sat under the ice cabinet, moved twice in four hours, and had evidently worked something out about Wednesdays that I am still catching up on.

Chronic offense-taking isn't performative outrage—it's a trauma response masquerading as oversensitivity.]]>

I used to think of a certain kind of person as a weather system. You know the type. You ask how the traffic was and somehow you have insulted their driving, their neighbourhood and their late mother. Everything lands as a slight. Everything requires a correction.

For years my take on this was simple and a bit smug. Attention seekers. People who enjoy the theatre of being wronged.

Then I started reading the actual psychology, and it turns out I had the story backwards. The people who seem offended by everything are rarely shopping for a fight. Most of them are running a security detail, and they have been running it since they were small.

When insults were the weather, everything looks like an insult

Here is the mechanism. If you grow up somewhere that regularly treats you as a target, your brain gets very good at spotting incoming fire. That is not a flaw. In the original environment it was survival. The problem is that the skill does not switch off when you move somewhere safer.

Psychologists call this hostile attribution bias, and it shows up early. Researchers followed around 1,300 children across nine countries and gave them scenarios where someone’s behaviour could be read as an accident or as deliberate. A shove in a corridor. A joke that could go either way. The children who consistently read hostile intent went on to show higher rates of persistent aggressive behaviour, even after accounting for how aggressive they had already been.

Two children see the same shove. One files it under accident, one files it under attack. Twenty years later, one of them is the adult who somehow takes offence at the weather report.

Being told you are too much is its own training

The other route in is quieter and I suspect more common.

Some people are not knocked around. They are simply corrected, constantly, about their own inner life. You are not upset. You are not tired. That did not hurt. Stop being dramatic. Clinicians call this an invalidating environment, a setting that consistently dismisses or punishes someone for expressing what they feel or need.

The theory behind that term was built to explain a specific clinical picture, so I would not go throwing it at your touchy colleague as a diagnosis. But the underlying logic travels. If your read on your own experience gets overruled a thousand times, you learn something ugly. You learn that your sense of things will not be taken seriously unless you make it loud.

And making it loud is exactly what the rest of us punish. We call it oversensitivity. We are reading the receipt and ignoring the purchase.

The tax the sensitive person pays

None of this is a free pass, and here is where it stops being sympathetic.

Researchers describe a disposition they call rejection sensitivity, meaning a tendency to anxiously expect rejection, spot it readily, and react hard when you think you have found it. People high in it tend to be less satisfied in their close relationships, and their partners report the same.

The trap is that the vigilance manufactures the thing it fears. You brace for the cold shoulder, so you go cold first. Your partner feels the chill and pulls back. Now you have evidence. Now the system that was built to protect your dignity has quietly started demolishing it.

I have watched this happen up close, over what I promise you was a genuinely neutral text message. There was no villain in that story. There was a very old alarm and a very ordinary Tuesday.

What actually helps when you are on the receiving end

Arguing about whether the offence was reasonable is a losing game. The alarm is not calibrated to this conversation. It was calibrated years ago, by somebody else.

Try naming the feeling without conceding the facts. Something like: I can see that landed badly, and I did not mean it that way. That costs you nothing on the question of intent, and it grants them something rare, which is agreement that their reaction was real. It does more work than an hour of you proving your innocence.

Be boringly consistent. Vigilance responds to evidence, not reassurance, and that takes months. You cannot talk someone out of a threat detector. You can only give it a long run of days where nothing bad happens.

And hold your line anyway. Understanding why someone snaps is not the same as accepting being snapped at. You can say plainly that you will not be shouted at and still mean everything above.

And if the thin skin is yours

Then start somewhere other than whether you were right. You often are. Slights are real, and some of the people telling you to calm down are exactly the ones worth watching.

The more useful question is what the alertness is costing you. Running security is expensive. It eats your Sundays. It makes you rehearse conversations that never happen and re-read messages for tone that was never there. My grandmother had a version of this. It made her formidable company. I think it also made her lonely.

So build a delay. When something lands wrong, wait a day before you respond. Graciousness has nothing to do with it. You are checking whether the feeling survives a night’s sleep. Usually it does not. The ones that do are worth taking seriously, and now you can take them seriously without the static.
